“The Pumpherston Hornpipe” C: Big Jim Sutherland

Currently without a turntable to listen to our copy of Gerald’s lovely LP “First Flight”, and without any other recording of this, I wasn’t able to confirm the transcription, which is just slightly out of norm. :-D But this I mean the bar counts. I’m hoping someone can confirm whether or not the A-part repeats or not? ~ which would be more usual for a 32 bar hornpipe. Tish’s transcription as given is ABB, with basically 4-bar 1st & 2nd endings for the B-part.

In the meantime I’ll try to see if I can chase up an earful of this to see how others have taken it. My inclination would be AABB…

↳ Posted by ceolachan on March 17th, 2014.

Pumpherston AABB

I checked out CDs of both Gerard Trimble and the Easy Club ‘Chance or Design’, and on both of these the first part is played twice. It’s Jim Sutherland himself playing on the latter, so that has to be the best authority.

↳ Posted by zoronic on August 15th, 2016.

Re: The Pumpherston

If you might have wondered how this tune got its name, the village of Pumpherston, in West Lothian, about 15 miles west of Edinburgh, was the centre of the Scottish Shale mining industry, with mining, refining, and later a brickworks to use up the red “spoil” from the mines. The spoil was also used for road building, notably the approaches to the first Forth Road Bridge, so the red hills, known as bings, gradually disappeared.
And yes, challenging tune, but gotta give it a go!

“The Pumpherston” hornpipe key

I’m curious, Gerald Trimble recorded this tune in G minor, but the transcriptions here are about evenly split between G minor and D minor.

Personally, I prefer the darkness of the D minor version, enjoying working it up on the B/C box, but was curious if there was another recording of the tune other than Gerald Trimble’s that might have been the inspiration for the transcriptions in D minor.

↳ Posted by Michael Eskin on September 27th, 2024.

Re: “The Pumpherston” hornpipe key

It’s a Jim Sutherland tune as you probably know.

In his tune book “The Flow Country”, it is notated with two flats… B and E which could be either B Flat or G minor.

I’d imagine he learned it from Jim when he was around the Edinburgh scene in the early eighties.

I’m assuming it’s G minor as opposed to B flat. Too early in the morning to disturb the neughbours. :-)

↳ Posted by 🎻 Melody Player 🎻 on September 27th, 2024.

Re: “The Pumpherston” hornpipe key

That explains the G minor versions, which are true to the original, but more curious about what motivated the D minor settings.

It’s probably just someone thought it sounded cool in D minor or sat better on their instrument in that key and posted a transposed version. I have not been able to find any reference to a recording in D minor so far.

Like I mentioned it does sit very well on the B/C box and provides for a wider pitch range than the G minor version without going into the third octave. I’ll probably have to master it in both keys to accommodate my local session players.

↳ Posted by Michael Eskin on September 27th, 2024.

Re: “The Pumpherston” hornpipe key

Whatever the key, I think it’s such a cool tune that it’s worth being able to play it in a couple of keys.
Thanks to you, Michael, for posting your Dm setting which brought the tune to my attention. I searched for the Easy Club version to play along with to find it there in Gm, which, for me, sat better on the mandolin and guitar.
It has a slightly different feel in Dm with the second part up the octave so I think I’ll learn it there too.

↳ Posted by DonaldK on September 28th, 2024.

Re: The Pumpherston

I see the discussion has been moved to the tune section. :-)
That’s OK but my comment seems a little daft now as everybody obviously realised that it is a Jim Sutherland tune originally in G minor. :-)
However, it did give me an excuse to dig out Jim’s tune book. So, I should revisit some of the great compositions therein.

Incidentally, Gerald Trimble spent some time in Edinburgh during the early eighties and could often be seen playing in sessions around town with the Easy Club boys and others.
We both happened to stay in the same B & B(The Royal Oak) at the 1982 Chester Folk Festival and I’m sure he will remember the very unsociable land lady there. :-(
As I recall, Hom Bru, Dab Hand, Andrew Cronshaw and others all stayed there that weekend too. It was a great weekend.
